content: The document titled Core Questions and Indicators for Monitoring WASH in Health Care Facilities in the Sustainable Development Goals was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) in 2018. It provides a framework for monitoring water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in health care facilities (HCFs) to support the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The publication emphasizes the critical role of WASH services in ensuring safe and quality health care, particularly in lowand middle-income countries where many facilities lack even basic WASH services. This deficiency compromises routine health services and infection prevention and control (IPC), hindering progress toward universal health coverage, reducing maternal and neonatal mortality, and achieving other health-related SDGs. The document outlines core indicators and questions to monitor WASH services in HCFs, including definitions for basic water, sanitation, hygiene, health care waste management, and environmental cleaning. These indicators aim to provide harmonized data collection tools that can be used globally to classify facilities based on service levels and track progress over time. The indicators are designed to be applicable across various facility types and settings, from small rural clinics to large tertiary hospitals. Key findings from a 2015 WHO and UNICEF report revealed significant gaps in WASH services in HCFs in lowand middle-income countries. For example, nearly 40% of facilities lacked water supplies within 500 meters, 19% had no access to improved sanitation, and 35% lacked handwashing facilities. These gaps highlight the urgent need for improved WASH services to enhance the quality of care, reduce health care-associated infections, and improve staff morale and patient satisfaction. The document also emphasizes the importance of leadership from the health sector, technical input from the WASH sector, and political commitment from governments and partners to improve WASH services in HCFs. It provides a set of core questions for data collection, which can be supplemented with additional questions for more detailed assessments. These questions are intended to be relevant in all countries and settings, focusing on the minimum criteria for basic WASH services. The publication acknowledges the contributions of the WASH in HCF Expert Group and the Global Task Team on monitoring WASH in HCFs in the SDG era. It also highlights the need for globally comparable data to monitor progress and improve WASH services in HCFs. The document aligns with WHO guidelines on IPC and provides recommendations for harmonized monitoring to support the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
